title: Chapter 70 – Heng's Trial
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Cheng Yun]

Cheng Yun has walked a great many prisoners to a great many halls, and he has never once been comfortable doing it.

It is not the prisoners. He has found, in nineteen years, that most of them are merely people who made a decision that cost more than they thought. It is the walking. It is the long cold corridor, the guards at either shoulder, the clean flat sound of boots on stone, and the quiet knowledge that at the end of it, someone he does not know will weigh a man's life against the Sect's convenience and write the sum in a book.

This morning the prisoner is carried.

The chair is black lacquer, with red silk cushions, and four Enforcement Hall bearers in gray at its poles. In it, propped upright by a rolled blanket, sits Zhao Heng, of Red Ridge. He is a man of middle years, pale, gaunt, with a high forehead and a mouth that has settled into a thin straight line. He has been a patient man all his life. It shows. He sits in the swaying chair with his hands folded on his knees and his eyes half closed, as if he were being borne to a feast.

He has not spoken since the cells.

"Inspector." It is the senior bearer, a stolid, middle-aged man. "The Hall is ready."

"Then let us not keep it waiting."

The great doors of the Hall of Open Session swing wide.

It is a long, high room, windowless, lit by lamps hung in rows from the rafters, floored in black stone polished to a mirror. A dais at the far end holds three chairs. A bench along the left wall holds the witnesses. A rail along the right holds the gallery, where perhaps two hundred disciples of the Outer Court sit shoulder to shoulder in their gray robes, watching in a hush that sounds like held breath.

Three Elders, thinks Cheng Yun. A Sect-wide trial, with three. It is a courtesy to Red Ridge. Or a warning.

Duan sits in the left chair, in iron-gray, head of the Enforcement Hall: a large, heavy, square-shouldered man with a close-cropped skull and a jaw like a gate. Shen Wuye sits in the right, in white, the Arbiter, still and lean and unreadable as a stone in a river. And in the center, in the deep blue of the Outer Affairs Hall, sits Fang, a smooth, comfortable, silver-haired man with ink on his sleeve and a face that has never in its life been caught frowning.

Duan wants a hanging. Shen wants a ruling. Fang wants it over by supper. He bows to the dais. Three men, three appetites. And the prisoner between them, like a bone.

He takes his place by the bench. He does not look at the gallery.

He does not need to. He has felt it from the door: the tall, plain figure at the end of the witness bench, in a dark blue tunic with a gray hem, hands folded, back very straight, with a bandage on one wrist. Lin Wenyuan has not turned his head. He has not shifted. He sits like a man who has come a very long way to say a single thing, and means to say it once.

* * *

Zhao Bei goes first.

It is brief. Cheng Yun has seen the Sect try a hundred cases, and this is the kind he likes best, the plain kind, with no one pretending. The steward of Red Ridge is led in by two guards, a broad, shaven-headed woman of forty-five with a face like a cliff. She stands in the center of the black floor and gives her name. She does not weep. She does not argue.

Duan reads the charges. They are long. The raising of sixty armed men against an affiliated clan without Court leave. The burning of a granary. The taking of nineteen prisoners. The unlawful entry of Green Pine Hill by night, under arms, in the service of a hidden sect. He reads them with a slow, grinding precision, like a man turning a mill.

"How do you plead?"

"I did as I was told," says Zhao Bei. Her voice is flat. "By my master. I had a list."

"A list."

"Of the Lin clan's children. With names." The shaven head turns, slowly, toward the bench. "I did not hurt them. I want that known. I took the granary, and I was beaten, and sixty men died in a trench I did not dig. I did not touch a child."

"We will hear the witness," says Shen.

Wenyuan rises.

He crosses the floor with a steady step, and bows, exactly, to the three chairs, and gives his name and his clan. He speaks for six minutes. Cheng Yun times it, from habit. It is a clean, spare, unhurried account: the night of the new moon, the unlocked gate, the trench, the count of the dead. At the end, Duan asks him if the woman struck a child. He says no. He says that she held a man's blade back from a girl of nine at the culvert, and was struck for it by her own captain.

He does not say it to help her. Cheng Yun sees that at once. He says it because it is true, and because he is a man who cannot leave a true thing unsaid.

That is a good man, thinks Cheng Yun. I wonder what it has cost him to be one.

The verdict takes eleven breaths. The mines of the Gray Peak. Twenty years. Her family retains its name. Zhao Bei bows, and goes out between her guards without a backward look, and in the gallery, somewhere to the left, a single woman begins very quietly to cry.

Next, thinks Cheng Yun, and sets his hand on the arm of Heng's chair.

* * *

The man in the chair does not stand.

He cannot. Cheng Yun has read the Healers' notes. A foundation cracked by a child of nine, a body held together for ten months by white tonic and spite, and a cure, a terrible cure, given on the eve of a siege by a man who is now dead. Heng can sit. He can speak. He can, with effort, turn his head. He cannot walk. He has lived in the chair since the autumn.

"Zhao Heng," says Duan. "Late Foundation. Head of the Zhao house of Red Ridge. Charged with conspiracy to seize by force the lands and works of the Lin clan of Green Pine Hill, in league with a proscribed sect, with the knowing use of its servants and its poisons, and with the unlawful testing of a child of the Register." He pauses. "Do you deny it?"

"No," says Heng.

His voice is a surprise. It is a light, dry, pleasant voice, a little hoarse, the voice of a man who might, in a different life, have taught poetry. It carries to the back of the hall without effort.

"I confessed in the courtyard of Green Pine Hill, before the Arbiter. I confess again. I raised the men. I wrote to the traitor. I took the cure." A faint, dry smile. "I should like it recorded that I did all of it knowingly, and that I regret only the result."

A murmur runs along the gallery.

"The Court notes that." Duan's voice is heavy. "The Court notes, also, that the accused is a man of rank, of intelligence, and of great cunning, and that a confession given freely before a witness is a confession given to avoid the cells. We have heard it before." He leans forward. "The Enforcement Hall asks death."

There it is, thinks Cheng Yun.

Fang coughs delicately. "The Outer Affairs Hall observes that the Zhao lands, being now under the Court, are quite adequately secured. And that the accused has no other family of rank who might..." He considers the phrase. "...resent the outcome. It is the view of this Hall that a sentence of confinement, with the usual guards, would satisfy the Sect's interest."

"Confinement," says Duan, "is not justice."

"It is economy."

"It is not..."

"The Arbiter," says Shen Wuye, "would like to hear from the accused."

The two men fall silent.

It is not a loud voice. Shen has never been loud. He sits in his white robe with his hands folded in his sleeves, and he looks at Heng with the long, steady, uninflected gaze of a man who has weighed ten thousand cases and has no particular wish to be hurried through this one.

"Zhao Heng," he says. "You have confessed to everything that can be proved. It was a clever confession. It leaves nothing for a trial to find. I should like to know why."

Heng is quiet for a moment.

"Because I am dying," he says, pleasantly. "The foundation is cracked. The cure was a stopgap. I have a year, perhaps two. I do not wish to spend them in argument." He tilts his head. "And because I have something that I wish to sell."

The hall goes quite still.

Ah, thinks Cheng Yun.

* * *

It is, he reflects afterward, one of the most skillful things he has ever seen.

Heng does not raise his voice. He does not bargain. He sits in the swaying chair, with his thin hands folded on the red silk, and he talks, in his dry soft voice, for a very long time, and the three Elders listen. It is not a speech. It is a sort of slow unfolding, like a man laying out cards.

"The Lin clan of Green Pine Hill," he says, "holds a thing the Court has not understood. You have called it a Garden. The Garden is not the thing. The Garden is a porch."

Duan stirs.

"I know, because I have read the Precepts. Not the public ones. The ninth, which says that a work of the Founder may not be held by an affiliated clan." The dry smile. "I invoked it, in the courtyard, as a pretext. It was not a pretext. It is true. And I know what the Founder built, and why he put it where he did. I know where it ends." He lets a moment pass. "It does not end at the Garden."

"Where does it end?" says Shen.

"Under the fortieth step."

It is a small sound, in a large hall. But Cheng Yun has been standing beside the witness bench for an hour, and he sees, with great clarity, what it does.

In the gallery, a stir. A faint, sharp rustle, like leaves in an unexpected wind. The two old Keepers at the back of the room have lifted their heads. And on the dais, Fang's comfortable face has, for the first time in Cheng Yun's experience, lost its ease.

He knows, thinks Cheng Yun. Fang knows what is under the fortieth step.

"I know," says Heng, "whose key opens it. I know how many tried, before. I know what was done to them." He does not look at the Elders. He looks at the lamps. "I will tell the Court all of it. Every name. Every date. The whole of the Founder's work, as it has come down to me, which is a great deal more than the Court has." A beat. "In exchange for my life. And a master."

"A master?" says Duan, sharply.

"A Sect disciple is answerable to his house, not to the Hall." Heng's smile has become a little weary. "I have a few months. I wish to spend them reading. I wish to spend them, if the Sect permits, in the Library, under the roof of an Elder who understands what I am offering. And I wish to be left alone by the people who would prefer I did not offer it."

The people who would prefer, thinks Cheng Yun, and his stomach turns slowly over.

He has seen it. He saw it a quarter-hour ago, when the man began to speak, a thin black thread at the base of the throat, just above the red silk collar, no wider than a hair. It is not visible to the eye. It is only visible to an inspector who has spent nineteen years looking at the places where a body does not match its confession.

It has grown.

It was a hair, at the start. It is a finger's width now. It is creeping, with great slowness, up the side of Heng's neck, toward the jaw. And the man's smile is a little tighter than it was, and his breath is a little shorter, and his thin fingers on the arm of the chair have begun, very slightly, to tremble.

A mark, thinks Cheng Yun. Written into him when he took the cure.

The same one that killed the watcher.

He does not know how he knows. He has not seen the watcher. He has only read Hu's note, sent by a Lin rider, on the second day of the Register, folded in a scrap of cloth: A Blood Shadow thread. It kills when it is asked a question. Look at the throat.

"I would like it recorded," says Heng, a little faintly, "that this is not a threat."

"It is a very good threat," says Duan.

"It is an offer." The pale lips tighten. "I have been..."

He stops.

It is a tiny pause. But the black line has reached the hinge of the jaw, and it is moving now, a little faster, and a single bead of sweat has run down from his hairline and dropped onto the red silk. He draws a breath. It rattles.

"Elder," says Cheng Yun, quietly, to the air, "the prisoner is..."

"I claim him."

The voice is a dry, light, gentle one, pitched not much above conversation. It comes from the gallery, from the east rail, where the Elders who are not sitting in judgment have taken their places. A figure has risen there. It is a lean, scholarly man in a gray robe, with a long beard and tired eyes, and a hand lifted, palm outward, in the old gesture of the Open Door.

"Elder Qin Hao," says Fang, with a flicker of something very like alarm.

"By the ancient right." The scholar does not raise his voice. "Before sentence is read, any Elder may open his door to an accused man, and take him into his house, as a disciple, for the remainder of his days. His crimes become his master's to answer. His justice, his silence, and his life are his master's to keep." He lowers his hand. "I have not used it in forty years. I should like to use it now."

For a long moment, no one speaks.

Duan rises, slowly, with a face like a thundercloud. "Elder Qin. The accused has confessed to treason."

"He has."

"He has had a Blood Shadow thread in his throat for three weeks, by the look of it. He has been written to die. You propose to take such a man into your house?"

"I propose," says Qin Hao mildly, "to take such a man into my house because he has been written to die." A small, dry, courteous smile. "A man whose silence has been bought with a thread in the throat is a man to whom no one in this room has yet had the chance to speak. I would like to. In my own study. With the door shut." He inclines his head to the dais. "I will take responsibility for him. All of it. If he flees, I will answer. If he kills, I will answer. If he speaks, I shall write it down."

A shield, thinks Cheng Yun. A very old one.

He watches the black line on Heng's neck.

It has stopped.

It sits at the angle of the jaw, with a faint, pulsing shimmer, like a thing that has been shown a door and is thinking about it. Qin Hao has not moved. But there is a small silver pin in his raised hand, no longer than a grain of rice, that Cheng Yun had not seen him take from his sleeve, and the air round Heng's chair has the cold, clear, faintly sweet feeling of a talisman at work.

He came prepared, he thinks.

He knew.

"The Arbiter," says Shen Wuye, "finds the claim in order."

* * *

The sentence takes forty minutes to compose.

It is a messy business, a compromise, the kind of thing Cheng Yun has watched the Sect make a hundred times. Duan does not get his hanging. Fang does not get his supper. Heng is not sentenced to death. He is not set free. He is committed, for the remainder of his days, to the house of the Elder Qin Hao, to be held in the cold cells of the Library Annex under the master's own seal, and not to be questioned by any blood-reader of the Enforcement Hall except by the master's leave.

"Cold cells," says Duan, heavily. "It is a death sentence by another road."

"It is a sentence of quiet," says Qin Hao. "He will be warm enough. He has been warm all his life."

Heng, in his chair, has gone very white. But he is smiling, and the black thread at his jaw is quiet, and as the bearers lift his chair, he turns his head, a very little, toward the witness bench. His dry light eyes pass over Wenyuan, and over Cheng Yun, and fix on a point on the far wall.

"Elder," he says. His voice is a thread. "I have a request."

"Speak."

"There is a boy. In the Outer Court. A disciple of the first year." A very faint pause. "Lin Jian. I would like to see him."

A murmur runs along the gallery like a sigh.

Wenyuan has half risen from the bench. His face is the color of paper.

"He is a child," says Qin Hao.

"He is the one who cracked my foundation." Heng's voice is perfectly gentle. "I would like to look at him, once, with my eyes, before I begin to read." He closes them. "I think he will want to know what I have to say."

"It is not within the Court's power to compel a disciple," says Shen.

"I do not ask it." The thin hands unfold on the red silk. "I only ask that it be put to him."

The doors of the Hall open. The bearers carry the chair out, in a swaying, unhurried procession, and the Elder of the Library walks behind it, with his hand lifted and his tired face composed, like a man following a coffin.

The silence that follows has a weight.

"The Court is adjourned," says Fang, with relief, "for the matter of Zhao Heng." He rises. "The Inspector will remain. There is a further matter."

Ah, thinks Cheng Yun again, and stands very still.

* * *

It takes place in a small room off the great hall, with a table and three chairs and no windows.

Duan has taken the head. He sits with his big hands flat on the wood, and a thin file of papers in front of him. He has not asked Cheng Yun to sit. Shen is at the far end, in his white robe, with his hands in his sleeves and his eyes on nothing.

"Your report," says Duan, "of the fourth month."

"Yes, Elder."

"It concerns the escort of the registered disciple Lin Jian, from Green Pine Hill to the Register. It states..." He lifts a page. "At the ford of the Gray Thread, the party was attacked by four Blood Shadow remnants. They were repelled by the escort, in the person of the Inspector, with no loss to the Court." He sets it down. "Is that accurate?"

"It is."

"You killed four Blood Shadow hunters. Three Drips and a ninth-stage, at the ford. Alone."

"Yes."

"By what means?"

"By sword, Elder."

"And pin?"

It is a very small word. It falls into the room like a coin into a pool.

"A ferryman reported on the fourth day," says Duan, "that a stretch of the river had been, in his words, set with iron. A Hall patrol went to look. They found six hollow pins in the stepping-stones, with wax caps. They found a ledge, undermined and broken. They found four broken glass jars, of a type made by one workshop, in one city, for one customer." He turns a page. "They found one man, dead, with a thread of Qi through the ribs so fine that the Healer thought it a needle. And the wounds on three others, none of which, I am told, were made by a sword."

Cheng Yun says nothing.

"A Qi Refining ninth-stage Blood Shadow hunter does not die of a pin in the foot," says Duan. "It requires a very great deal of preparation. It requires a mind that has thought about the ford for three days. It does not require a mid-Foundation inspector with a sword." He leans back. "It requires a child."

"Elder..."

"I do not accuse you." The big face is expressionless. "I observe. You have written a false report. You have done it knowingly. You have done it, I think, to shield a disciple of the first year who was also, I note, a witness in the case you were escorting him to. Who has a most unusual cultivation. Who is, as of the noon bell, the most discussed name in the Outer Court." A pause, heavy as a stone. "It is a matter for the Hall."

Yes, thinks Cheng Yun.

He has known it since the ford. He has known it every hour since, riding the box of the cart, writing the report in his own neat hand, by candlelight, at the inn at Willow Bend. He had written it three times. He had burned two. He had thought: There is a man in the Outer Court who limps and has never asked me for anything. There is a boy who reads like a third-layer and fights like a ninth. There is a sketch of a child's hand in the Arbiter's desk, and a deputy who has written cause unknown. There is a hill that has been very carefully lied to, by a number of honest people.

He had thought: It is the first false line I have ever written.

"It was a judgment of the moment," he says. "The boy was a child. The attackers were Blood Shadow. I did not wish..."

"You wished to protect him."

"Yes."

"From the Court?"

"From the attention," says Cheng Yun. It is true. It is the truest thing he has said all day.

He thinks Duan will strike him. It is in the set of the big shoulders. But it is Shen who speaks, in his light, even, unhurried voice, without turning his head.

"The Inspector has served the Court nineteen years," he says. "He has declined promotion three times. He has not, in that time, written a false figure. I have read his ledgers. I have not found one." The long hand lifts a little. "I would like to know what has changed."

"Nothing, Arbiter."

"Something."

Cheng Yun looks at the table. At the file. At the thin black line of the grain in the wood, running from edge to edge like a seam.

"A man may be loyal to the Sect," he says slowly, "and still believe that there are things in it that ought not to be handed a child. I audited a clan. I found no false figure. I found a house in which every person was telling the truth to the limit of what they could afford." He lifts his eyes. "I did not wish to be the one who made them afford more."

The silence is very long.

"Your rank," says Duan at last, "is suspended pending review. You will not take an escort or an audit. You will report to the Hall each morning." The big hand lifts the page, and lets it fall. "If the review finds you have lied again, you will answer for it."

"Yes, Elder."

"Go."

He goes. He walks out through the great Hall, across the black floor where, an hour ago, a man was carried in to be hanged and carried out to be kept. There is nobody in it now but a servant with a broom. The lamps are being put out, one by one.

At the door, a thin, tall figure in a dark blue tunic is standing with his back to the light. He has been waiting. His bandaged hand hangs at his side.

"Inspector," says Lin Wenyuan.

"Patriarch."

"I heard." The Patriarch's voice is quiet and level. "A guard told me, in the corridor. I am sorry."

"Do not be." Cheng Yun finds, to his considerable surprise, that he means it. "It is the first thing I have done in nineteen years that I would do again."

Wenyuan looks at him. It is a long, grave, measuring look, the look of one honest man at another across a table of figures that do not balance.

"Heng has asked for my son," he says.

"Yes."

"I do not know what to do."

"No." Cheng Yun draws his cloak about him. Beyond the doors, the afternoon is bright and cold. "Nor do I. But I think that boy will not wait to be told."
